name: Savings plan
seoTitle: Savings plan Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Savings plan: work out savings plan from the planning for.... A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The savings plan calculator returns savings plan from the 16 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. It is built for a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Savings plan calculator work?
sections.html:
The Savings plan calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports savings plan in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the planning for... (Your savings plan's target), the planning for... (Your savings plan's target), the planning for... (Your savings plan's target) and the planning for... (Your savings plan's target).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the Savings plan calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Savings plan=(my savings plan's target, I'm planning to put aside..., var rep, var plan, var mode, planning for..., planning for..., planning for..., repeatedly increased by..., deposit #1, deposit #2, deposit #3, deposit #4, deposit #5, deposit #6, deposit #7)
Final balance=((my savings plan's target, I'm planning to put aside..., var rep, var plan, var mode, planning for..., planning for..., planning for..., repeatedly increased by..., deposit #1, deposit #2, deposit #3, deposit #4, deposit #5, deposit #6, deposit #7))
Periodic deposit=((my savings plan's target, I'm planning to put aside..., var rep, var plan, var mode, planning for..., planning for..., planning for..., repeatedly increased by..., deposit #1, deposit #2, deposit #3, deposit #4, deposit #5, deposit #6, deposit #7))

Dep first=((my savings plan's target, I'm planning to put aside..., var rep, var plan, var mode, planning for..., planning for..., planning for..., repeatedly increased by..., deposit #1, deposit #2, deposit #3, deposit #4, deposit #5, deposit #6, deposit #7))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Savings plan calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the planning for... — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Savings plan calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns savings plan, derived from the planning for.... Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Savings plan calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the planning for..., which is 16 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter my savings plan's target in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. My savings plan's target opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Savings plan calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
